title: Game 11: Capablanca–Janowski
subtitle: Open lines against a queenside king

steps.title: An Exchange Ruy Lopez with opposite-side castling

narration.say: Capablanca has White against Janowski at St. Petersburg in 1914. White exchanges on c6 and develops the other knight.
White supports the centre and develops the bishop. Black exchanges it, opening the f-file.
White castles kingside. Black castles queenside.

steps.title: Attack the wing where the king stands

narration.say: White prepares queenside pawn advances while Black manoeuvres the knight.
White recaptures with the rook. Black plays b6.
White opens the queenside and establishes the knight on d5.

steps.title: Bring the queen and rooks together

narration.say: Black’s knight manoeuvres. White repositions the rook and queen.
White can now challenge the centre and open more lines.

exercise.prompt: White to move. Advance the d-pawn to open the centre.

steps.title: Pawn breaks make the attack concrete

narration.say: White prepares pressure on the c-file. Black exchanges in the centre and moves the knight to f4.

exercise.prompt: White to move. Attack the queen on d6 with a pawn advance.

narration.say: White recaptures the knight with the e-pawn. Black captures d5 with the queen.
The c-pawn advances with check, then takes the rook on d7.
White advances the d-pawn. Black brings the rook to e8.

exercise.prompt: White to move. Advance the passed pawn again.

narration.say: White brings the queen to c6. Black resigns.
The game ends at the final move recorded in the book. No extra moves are added.
White did not attack with pawns alone. The rooks and queen were repositioned before the central breakthrough.
The c-pawn won a rook, and the d-pawn opened the final route for the queen.
Opposite-side castling can make pawn advances urgent, but coordination still determines whether they succeed.
